# Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 86 (Bu-Vb Pc86)
**ID:** Bu-Vb Pc86
**Section:** Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga (bu-vb)
**Collection:** Vinaya
**Title (Pali):** Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 86
**Title (English, from literature):** Making an inappropriate needle case

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
**Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 86** (*Sūcighara-sikkhāpada*) is the eighty-sixth training rule in the Pācittiya chapter of the Theravāda *Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga* [SuttaCentral]. The rule establishes an offence for a Buddhist monk who makes or has made a needle case (*sūcighara*) fashioned from forbidden materials, specifically bone, ivory, or horn; the monk is required to break the illicit object and confess the transgression [SuttaCentral; Horner; Hüsken 1997]. In analytical classifications of Vinaya injunctions, Ute Hüsken notes that this precept belongs to the category of *bhedanaka-pācittiya* ("involving breaking"), wherein an object made from impermissible materials must be destroyed, mirroring the restorative procedures found in the *nissaggiya pācittiya* rules [Hüsken 1997]. Michael Radich cites this prohibition against fancy needle cases alongside provisions concerning begging bowls, high beds, and stuffed furniture as monastic regulations intended to discipline bodily comportment and uphold ascetic austerity [Radich 2007].
Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral demonstrate that this training rule is shared widely across early Buddhist monastic traditions, appearing in the Theravāda Bhikkhu and Bhikkhunī Pātimokkhas, the *Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga* (Pācittiya 162), and corresponding Pācittiya sections of the Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsaṅghika, Dharmaguptaka, and Kāśyapīya Vinayas preserved in Chinese, Sanskrit, and Tibetan [SuttaCentral]. Computational text-reuse analysis via DharmaNexus corroborates extensive formulaic overlap with 91 other Pali texts, matching most strongly with Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Nissaggiya Pācittiya 22, the *Katāpattivāra* of the *Parivāra*, Khandhaka texts (such as Kd 6, Kd 16, and Kd 1), and contiguous Vibhaṅga rules (Pc 88 and Pc 89), alongside cross-linguistic alignment with Tibetan Vinaya texts including the *Vinayasaṃgraha* [DharmaNexus]. Modern English translations include that of Bhikkhu Brahmali [SuttaCentral].
